title: Organic Chemistry
tagline: Explore carbon compounds, functional groups, nomenclature and key organic reactions.

overview.intro: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds, which are numerous due to carbon’s tetravalency and ability to form chains, rings and multiple bonds. This chapter introduces unique nature of carbon, homologous series, IUPAC nomenclature basics, isomerism, and the structure and reactions of important classes such as alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, alcohols and carboxylic acids. Emphasis is placed on functional groups, general formulae and characteristic reactions relevant to ICSE.

learningOutcomes: Explain tetravalency and catenation as reasons for the vast number of organic compounds.
Identify homologous series, functional groups and general formulae.
Apply basic IUPAC nomenclature and recognise structural isomerism.
Describe properties and reactions of alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, ethanol and ethanoic acid.
Write balanced equations for combustion, substitution, addition and esterification reactions.

learn.title: Unique Nature of Carbon and Homologous Series

blocks.text: Carbon forms a very large number of compounds because of tetravalency (valency four) and catenation, the ability to form strong covalent bonds with other carbon atoms to create chains and rings. Carbon also forms single, double and triple bonds, leading to diverse structures and properties.

A homologous series is a family of organic compounds with the same functional group and general formula, where successive members differ by a CH2 unit. Members show a gradation in physical properties and similar chemical properties. Examples include alkanes (CnH2n+2), alkenes (CnH2n) and alkynes (CnH2n-2).

items: Catenation allows long chains and branched structures.
Functional group determines characteristic chemical reactions.
Successive homologues differ by 14 u in molecular mass (CH2).
Isomerism arises when compounds have same molecular formula but different structures.

blocks.text: IUPAC nomenclature provides a systematic way to name organic compounds based on the longest carbon chain, type of bonds and functional groups. Prefixes indicate substituents, the root indicates number of carbon atoms, and suffixes indicate saturation or functional group (e.g. -ane, -ene, -yne, -ol, -oic acid).

Structural isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements of atoms. At ICSE level, chain isomerism in simple hydrocarbons and position/functional variations in basic compounds may be introduced. Drawing and naming structures correctly helps distinguish isomers.

Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons containing only single C–C bonds and follow the general formula CnH2n+2. They are relatively less reactive and undergo substitution reactions with halogens in presence of sunlight and combustion in oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water.

Alkenes (CnH2n) contain at least one C=C double bond and alkynes (CnH2n-2) contain at least one C≡C triple bond; both are unsaturated hydrocarbons. They undergo addition reactions in which atoms add across the multiple bond, and they decolourise bromine water (a test for unsaturation under suitable conditions).

items.note: Addition reaction across the double bond in ethene.

blocks.text: Alcohols contain the hydroxyl functional group (–OH). Ethanol (C2H5OH) is a common alcohol that burns with a clean flame, reacts with sodium to liberate hydrogen, and undergoes dehydration to form ethene under suitable conditions. It is used as a solvent, fuel component and in beverages (in regulated contexts).

Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl functional group (–COOH). Ethanoic acid (acetic acid, CH3COOH) is a weak acid that turns blue litmus red, reacts with carbonates to release carbon dioxide, and reacts with ethanol in presence of concentrated sulphuric acid to form an ester (ethyl ethanoate) with a fruity smell, a reaction known as esterification.

items.meaning: An atom or group of atoms responsible for characteristic reactions of a compound.
A reaction in which atoms are added across a double or triple bond.
Reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol to form an ester and water.

blocks.text: Combustion of hydrocarbons and alcohols in sufficient oxygen produces carbon dioxide and water, releasing heat. Incomplete combustion may produce carbon monoxide or soot. Balanced equations for combustion require careful counting of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms.

Unsaturated hydrocarbons can be distinguished from saturated ones by addition reactions, such as decolourisation of bromine in an inert solvent (or bromine water under appropriate conditions). Ethanoic acid can be identified by its reaction with sodium carbonate (effervescence of CO2) and by ester formation with ethanol in presence of concentrated sulphuric acid.

items: Saturated compounds: mainly substitution; unsaturated: addition.
Esterification requires an acid catalyst (conc. H2SO4) and warming.
Write structural or condensed formulae clearly when naming compounds.
Handle organic substances carefully; many are flammable.

keyPoints: Carbon’s tetravalency and catenation explain the large number of organic compounds.
Homologous series members share a functional group and general formula, differing by CH2.
IUPAC names reflect carbon chain length, bonding and functional groups.
Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures.
Alkanes are saturated and undergo substitution; alkenes/alkynes are unsaturated and undergo addition.
Ethanol shows reactions of alcohols including combustion and reaction with sodium.
Ethanoic acid shows acidic properties and forms esters with alcohols.
Combustion products depend on oxygen supply; complete combustion gives CO2 and H2O.
Bromine decolourisation and ester smell are useful identification observations.
Balanced equations and correct functional group identification are essential.
examFocus: Define homologous series, functional group, isomerism and catenation.
Write general formulae and names for simple alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, alcohols and acids.
Distinguish saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons by reactions.
Write equations for substitution in methane, addition in ethene and esterification.
Describe properties and uses of ethanol and ethanoic acid.
Draw or interpret simple structural/condensed formulae.
State observations for bromine test and ester formation.

vocabulary.meaning: Branch of chemistry dealing with carbon compounds (with a few exceptions).
Ability of carbon atoms to form bonds with each other to make chains and rings.
A family of compounds with same functional group and general formula, differing by CH2.
An atom/group responsible for characteristic chemical reactions of a compound.
Existence of compounds with same molecular formula but different structures.
A saturated hydrocarbon with only single bonds, general formula CnH2n+2.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon with at least one C=C bond, general formula CnH2n.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon with at least one C≡C bond, general formula CnH2n-2.
A reaction in which one atom or group is replaced by another.
A reaction in which atoms add across a multiple bond.
Formation of an ester from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid with water.
Systematic method for naming organic compounds using standard rules.

questions.prompt: The general formula of alkanes is:
questions.explanation: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with only single bonds and follow CnH2n+2.
questions.commonMistake: CnH2n is the general formula for alkenes.

questions.prompt: Successive members of a homologous series differ by:
questions.explanation: Each successive homologue differs by one methylene (CH2) group.
questions.commonMistake: The mass difference between successive members is 14 u.

questions.prompt: Ethene decolourises bromine solution due to:
questions.explanation: Bromine adds across the carbon-carbon double bond in ethene.
questions.commonMistake: Alkanes undergo substitution, not addition, under normal conditions.

questions.prompt: The functional group in ethanoic acid is:
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group (-COOH).
questions.commonMistake: -OH is the functional group of alcohols.

questions.prompt: Esterification occurs when ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol in presence of:
questions.explanation: Concentrated sulphuric acid acts as catalyst and dehydrating agent in esterification.
questions.commonMistake: Warming is usually required along with the acid catalyst.

questions.prompt: Methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight to form chloromethane by:
questions.explanation: A hydrogen atom in methane is replaced by a chlorine atom in presence of sunlight.
questions.commonMistake: Sunlight is necessary for this substitution reaction.

questions.prompt: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures are called:
questions.explanation: Structural isomers differ in arrangement of atoms despite having identical molecular formulae.
questions.commonMistake: Homologues belong to the same series but have different molecular formulae.

questions.prompt: The IUPAC name of CH3-CH2-OH is:
questions.explanation: The compound has two carbon atoms and an -OH group, so its name is ethanol.
questions.commonMistake: Count the carbon atoms in the longest chain correctly.

questions.prompt: Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain at least one carbon-carbon ________ or triple bond.
questions.explanation: Alkenes have double bonds and alkynes have triple bonds, making them unsaturated.
questions.commonMistake: Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single bonds.

questions.prompt: The reaction of an alcohol with a carboxylic acid to form an ester is called ________.
questions.explanation: Esterification produces an ester and water, often with a fruity smell.
questions.commonMistake: Concentrated sulphuric acid is commonly used as catalyst.

questions.prompt: The ability of carbon atoms to form bonds with other carbon atoms is called ________.
questions.explanation: Catenation leads to long chains and rings in organic compounds.
questions.commonMistake: Tetravalency refers to carbon having valency four.

questions.prompt: What is a homologous series?
questions.answer: A homologous series is a group of organic compounds having the same functional group and general formula, in which successive members differ by a CH2 unit and show similar chemical properties with gradual change in physical properties.
questions.explanation: This definition includes composition, difference and property trends.
questions.commonMistake: Mention both similar chemical properties and gradation in physical properties.

questions.prompt: Write the equation for the combustion of methane in sufficient oxygen.
questions.explanation: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon produces carbon dioxide and water.
questions.commonMistake: Balance oxygen atoms on both sides of the equation.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons with one example each.
questions.answer: Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single carbon-carbon bonds, for example ethane (C2H6). Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain at least one double or triple carbon-carbon bond, for example ethene (C2H4). Saturated hydrocarbons generally undergo substitution reactions, while unsaturated ones undergo addition reactions.
questions.explanation: The type of bonding determines both classification and typical reactions.
questions.commonMistake: Give correct examples that match each category.

questions.prompt: State two chemical properties of ethanoic acid.
questions.answer: Ethanoic acid reacts with sodium carbonate or bicarbonate to produce carbon dioxide gas, water and sodium ethanoate, showing acidic character. It reacts with ethanol in presence of concentrated sulphuric acid on warming to form ethyl ethanoate (an ester) and water.
questions.explanation: These reactions demonstrate acidity and esterification.
questions.commonMistake: Include observations such as effervescence or fruity smell where relevant.

questions.prompt: Describe the substitution reaction of methane with chlorine and the addition reaction of ethene with bromine, including conditions and equations.
questions.answer: Methane reacts with chlorine in presence of sunlight to form chloromethane and hydrogen chloride by substitution: CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl (sunlight). Ethene reacts with bromine to form 1,2-dibromoethane by addition across the double bond: C2H4 + Br2 → C2H4Br2. The substitution requires light and replaces an atom, while addition breaks the double bond and adds atoms without releasing a small molecule.
questions.explanation: Conditions and bond changes distinguish the two reaction types.
questions.commonMistake: State sunlight for methane-chlorine reaction and the type of reaction for each.

questions.prompt: Explain esterification with an equation, conditions and observation. How can the ester be identified?
questions.answer: When ethanoic acid is warmed with ethanol in presence of a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid, ethyl ethanoate and water are formed: CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O. Concentrated sulphuric acid acts as catalyst and dehydrating agent. The ester formed has a characteristic sweet or fruity smell, which helps in its identification.
questions.explanation: Reactants, conditions, products and observation together describe esterification fully.
questions.commonMistake: Mention warming and concentrated sulphuric acid, not just mixing the reactants.

questions.prompt: Discuss the unique nature of carbon that leads to the formation of a large number of organic compounds.
questions.answer: Carbon has tetravalency, allowing it to form four covalent bonds with other atoms, including carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and halogens. It shows catenation, the ability to form strong bonds with other carbon atoms, resulting in long chains, branched chains and rings. Carbon can also form single, double and triple bonds, increasing structural variety. These features, along with isomerism and formation of stable covalent compounds, lead to an enormous number of organic compounds with diverse properties.
questions.explanation: Tetravalency, catenation and multiple bonding together explain carbon’s versatility.
questions.commonMistake: Include more than one reason; tetravalency alone is incomplete.

questions.prompt: A hydrocarbon decolourises bromine solution in carbon tetrachloride. What does this indicate about the hydrocarbon? Give one example.
questions.answer: Decolourisation of bromine indicates that the hydrocarbon is unsaturated, containing a carbon-carbon double or triple bond that undergoes an addition reaction with bromine. For example, ethene reacts with bromine to form 1,2-dibromoethane, removing the brown colour of bromine.
questions.explanation: Addition across multiple bonds consumes bromine, causing decolourisation.
questions.commonMistake: Saturated hydrocarbons do not decolourise bromine under these conditions without sunlight.

questions.prompt: Given the molecular formula C4H10, explain how more than one structure is possible and name the type of isomerism.
questions.answer: C4H10 can be arranged as a straight chain (butane, CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3) or as a branched chain (2-methylpropane). Both have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements and properties. This is an example of structural isomerism, specifically chain isomerism.
questions.explanation: Different carbon skeletons produce distinct compounds with the same formula.
questions.commonMistake: Draw or describe both structures to show the difference clearly.

questions.prompt: How would you chemically distinguish between ethanol and ethanoic acid? Give two tests with observations.
questions.answer: Add sodium carbonate solution to each: ethanoic acid produces brisk effervescence due to carbon dioxide gas, while ethanol shows no effervescence. Alternatively, add blue litmus: ethanoic acid turns blue litmus red, while ethanol does not change blue litmus. Another test is warming each with ethanoic acid/ethanol and concentrated sulphuric acid: a mixture containing both forms a fruity-smelling ester, but each alone with the catalyst does not produce that ester smell in the same way. The carbonate and litmus tests are clear distinguishing observations.
questions.explanation: Acidic behaviour of ethanoic acid provides reliable distinguishing reactions.
questions.commonMistake: Choose tests with clear, different observations for the two liquids.

questions.prompt: Why do alkenes undergo addition reactions whereas alkanes generally undergo substitution reactions?
questions.answer: Alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond with a reactive pi bond, which can open up to allow atoms to add across it, forming a saturated product. Alkanes have only strong single bonds and no such reactive multiple bond, so under typical conditions atoms replace hydrogen atoms rather than adding to the molecule, resulting in substitution reactions.
questions.explanation: The presence or absence of a multiple bond governs the main reaction pathway.
questions.commonMistake: Relate the reaction type to bond structure, not just to formula.
